On this view it is an ingredient that "partially realizes" the law, not a law and not a material field. So its time-dependence and non-uniqueness (a phase shift, a density matrix) are harmless, it counts as non-epistemic and ontic, and it can take part in constructive explanation. Each of these is argued informally, and the escape from PBR is by relabelling the ontic/epistemic distinction, not by engaging the theorem. | Read |
| [NOTE-162](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-162.md) v2 | French — Unitary inequivalence and structural realism | French answers Howard's objection that QFT's unitarily inequivalent representations leave the structural realist with non-isomorphic, competing structures. He offers two routes. The first is to adopt cut-off "conventional" QFT with Wallace, on which the inequivalence is an artefact or harmless. The second is to follow Ruetsche's Swiss Army Knife and treat the algebra as a modal structure spanning all representations. On that reading spontaneous symmetry breaking preserves the symmetry across the degenerate vacua, and the DHR analysis derives quantum statistics from the algebra. Adding Baker's criterion, on which a symmetry mapping between representations suffices for intertranslatability, removes the assumption behind the objection, and French ends with a third option that combines the two routes. Every step is an informal argument layered on others' technical results; the paper proves nothing itself. | Read |
| [NOTE-163](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-163.md) v2 | SEP — Mereology | The entry argues that no mereological principle, not even the partial-order core M (Reflexivity, Transitivity, Antisymmetry), is merely a fixing of the meaning of "part". It lays out the ladder M ⊂ MM (+Supplementation) ⊂ EM (+Strong Supplementation) ⊂ GEM (+Unrestricted Sum). GEM is "virtually" a complete Boolean algebra with zero removed, and it is reached from M by exactly three adequate pairings: Supplementation + Unrestricted Sum2, Strong Supplementation + Unrestricted Sum3, and Complementation + Unrestricted Sum1. The influential Simons (1987) pairing, Supplementation + Unrestricted Sum3, which the entry's own 2003 edition also used, does not yield GEM. | Read |
| [NOTE-166](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-166.md) v2 | Personal Identity and Ethics (SEP) | A survey, arguing no thesis of its own, of how three contested questions bear on ethics: which account of persistence is true (unique psychological continuity, Shoemaker and Parfit; or biological continuity and animalism, Olson and DeGrazia), whether identity or the psychological relations (continuity and/or connectedness) is what matters (Parfit's fission case), and whether metaphysics constrains ethics or the reverse. It traces these through prudential concern, responsibility, abortion (Marquis), death and brain-death criteria, dementia and advance directives (Dworkin vs Jaworska on Margo), and the separateness of persons (Rawls, Parfit, Nozick, Taurek, Sidgwick, Brink). Its main recurring finding is that the relation that fixes persistence and the relation that matters ethically keep coming apart. It concludes that all three questions remain open. | Read |
| [NOTE-172](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-172.md) v2 | Watson — On the philosophy of unsupervised learning | Watson argues that clustering, abstraction and generative modelling each come with an epistemic thesis (EC, EA, EG — we identify natural kinds, essential properties and unrealized possibilities via such algorithms or something like them), which he accepts. Each also comes with an ontological thesis (OC, OA, OG — these just *are* what the algorithms ought to find under ideal conditions), which he rejects because nothing guarantees they are effectively computable. He adds a pragmatic, context-relative view of natural kinds, and closes with the claim that unsupervised outputs are neither "objective" nor vacuous. They should be validated by error-statistical means: resampling stability, generalization of clusters to held-out data, out-of-sample likelihood, and train-on-synthetic scores. | Read |
| [NOTE-174](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-174.md) v2 | Rovelli — The relational interpretation (RQM) | Rovelli restates RQM as an ontology of sparse relative facts, which arise in interactions and are labelled by the interacting systems. Its one technical rule is that an amplitude W(b,a) gives the probability P = \|W\|² only when a and b are relative to the same system. That rule removes the clash between P_collapse = Σᵢ\|W(c,bᵢ)\|²\|W(bᵢ,a)\|² and P_unitary = \|ΣᵢW(c,bᵢ)W(bᵢ,a)\|² (eqs. 2–4). Decoherence makes some facts approximately label-independent ("stable"). ψ is a relative-state bookkeeping device, like a Hamilton–Jacobi function S. The price, which Rovelli states, is giving up "strong realism": values are not held at all times, may be held at different times for different systems, and there is no coherent global view and no quantum state of the universe. | Read |
| [NOTE-175](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-175.md) v2 | Chen — Realism about the Wave Function | A survey that sorts realist readings of the non-relativistic universal wave function into four ontological readings (a field on 3N-dimensional space, a multi-field on 3-space, properties of systems as in spacetime state realism, a Hilbert-space vector), two nomological ones (strong: time-independent and simple like the classical Hamiltonian; weak: a Humean best-system variable) and Maudlin's sui generis option. It tabulates their compatibility with BM, GRW0/m/f and S0/Sm and with high- versus low-dimensional fundamental space (Table 1, 10 of 56 cells "?"), and declares no winner. | Read |
| [NOTE-178](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-178.md) v2 | De Haro & Butterfield — Philosophy and Physics of Duality | The book gives a formal Schema: a duality is an isomorphism between the "model roots" (state space, quantities, dynamics) of two models of a common-core bare theory, with values and dynamics matching. It pairs this with an interpretative condition: duals are physically equivalent iff (A) they are duals and (B) i1 = i2∘d. On that basis it argues four things. First, there are no genuine cases of in-principle underdetermination in the examples, and a cautious realist can commit to the common core. Second, dualities do not favour structural realism. Third, duality is formally incompatible with ontological emergence, except "beside" it (AdS/CFT's RG direction), via effective dualities, or epistemically. Fourth, quasi-dualities motivate a "geometric view" on which models are charts on a successor theory's moduli space. | Read |
| [NOTE-180](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-180.md) v4 | Clark & Chalmers — The Extended Mind | The paper argues from a functionalist parity claim that a process or standing state which would count as cognitive if it happened in the head counts as cognitive when an external resource carries it, provided the resource is actively coupled to the organism here and now. Otto's notebook entry is its example of such a standing belief. From this it infers, in one paragraph, that the self extends too. The four "criteria" for a coupled resource (constancy, direct availability, automatic endorsement, and the admittedly "arguable" past conscious endorsement) are offered as the features that make the paradigm case clear. The paper explicitly says they are not necessary and sufficient conditions. | Read |
| [NOTE-182](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-182.md) v2 | Arsiwalla et al. — Pregeometry and formal language | A programmatic essay with no construction, theorem or model of its own. It argues that inferential justification in a materialist ontology regresses without end (§3), that a "coherentist" constructivism escapes the regress, and that Wheeler's pregeometry is therefore best read as "structureless structure": the types and compositional rules of a computational language such as homotopy type theory (§§4, 6). Every construction of space from such rules that it points to is in the authors' own earlier papers ([13, 17, 18]) or is promised as "a forthcoming publication" (fn. 1, p. 3). | Read |
| [NOTE-187](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-187.md) | On the Evolution, Science, and Metaphysics of Consciousness | Veit's reply to five commentaries on *A Philosophy for the Science of Animal Consciousness* (2023). Its main new content is the metaphysics the book left to one paragraph. He says hedonic "feel" is *identical* with a valence system: "a common currency of sharing evaluative information across multiple control systems". The currency metaphor, he says, is "not Cartesian but cybernetic" (p. 10). He keeps the word "qualia", arguing that Cartesians have no "definitional rights" (p. 9), and he insists the pathological complexity thesis (PCT) is compatible with any metaphysics, dualism and panpsychism included (p. 9). Against his other critics, he defends a bottom-up evolutionary method that uses human data (de Weerd); a naturalism that is neither autopoietic nor biopsychist (Sachs); evaluation-first over prediction-first, consciousness as an adaptation, and graded, partial unity (Suzuki); and the link to welfare science (Chincarini). | Read |
| [NOTE-188](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-188.md) v2 | The Weirdness of the World | The book's thesis is that every viable theory of how consciousness fits into the cosmos, and of the cosmos's basic structure, is both "bizarre" (contrary to common sense) and "dubious" (not rationally compelling). So "something that seems almost too crazy to believe must be true" (p. 4), and credence should be spread across the bizarre options. Examples of those options are that the United States is conscious (if materialism is true), that we are sims or Boltzmann brains (a 0.1–1% credence), that space is transcendentally ideal, that almost every act causes almost every future event, and that there is no fact about snail consciousness. Its only positive empirical results are three self-experiments against solipsism (for example, 17 of 19 decisive chess games lost, p < .001). Everything else is informal argument. | Read |
| [NOTE-189](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-189.md) | Ontic Structural Realism and Economics | Ross argues that OSR, usually motivated only by fundamental physics, is also the right ontology for a mature special science, economics. The progress of economic theory from Jevons through Hicks–Allen (1934), Samuelson (1947), Debreu (1959) and Arrow (1965) consists in steadily removing psychological, individual-level hypotheses. Its basic objects are optimisation problems, above all games, which are "mathematical structures … whose relata are distinguished as such by the mathematical representations … just like quarks and bosons" (§3). So OSR, joined with an assumption that science is unified, gets consilient support from outside physics. Individuals, in physics and in economics, are "book-keeping devices". | Read |
| [NOTE-190](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-190.md) | Real Patterns | A pattern is real in some data "if there is a description of the data that is more efficient than the bit map, whether or not anyone can concoct it" (p. 34). This is Chaitin's incompressibility definition of randomness turned around (p. 32). Dennett uses the criterion, with the Game of Life's gliders and eaters as the stepping stone (pp. 37–42), to defend "mild realism" about beliefs. Folk psychology tracks a real, noisy pattern of enormous predictive leverage. Two rival interpretations can be "different, but equally real, patterns" with no deeper fact to settle between them (p. 49). | Read |
| [NOTE-191](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-191.md) | Patterns All the Way Up | Ladyman restates the Ladyman–Ross metaphysics as fifteen theses drawn from scientific practice. The existence criterion is "to be is to be a real pattern", a pattern that "indispensibly figures in projectible generalisations" (p. 2). Realism is realism about natural modal structure, which is "absolute" in formal mode but "domain and scale-dependent" in material mode (thesis 4). There is no single hierarchy of levels and no assumed fundamental level (theses 10–11, fn. 9). Ontology is effective and scale-relative (thesis 12). Scientific real patterns are lossy compressions, unlike the Game of Life's; the ideal gas laws use 3 degrees of freedom for ~10²³ (thesis 14). He quotes ETMG's Principle of Naturalistic Closure verbatim and calls it "problematic" because it refers to fundamental physics (p. 8). | Read |
| [NOTE-192](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-192.md) | Science, Metaphysics and Structural Realism | Ladyman argues that structural realism should be metaphysically, not epistemically, revisionary. He gives three grounds. Quantum statistics leaves the individuality of particles underdetermined: permutation invariance gives 3 two-particle states, not 4, so probabilities are 1/3 rather than 1/4 (p. 62). Entangled states give non-supervenient relations that refute Humean supervenience (pp. 71–73). The hole argument blocks point-based substantivalism (pp. 68–69). He proposes that science describes "the modal structure of the phenomena" (p. 73), with modal realism supplying the no-miracles intuition. The paper ends non-eliminatively: "the phenomena have structure but they are not structure" (p. 74). | Read |
| [NOTE-193](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-193.md) | Category-theoretic structure and radical ontic structural realism | Bain argues that the "relations without relata" objection to radical OSR depends on defining structure set-theoretically, where a relation is a subset of X × X. If a structure is instead "an object in a category", its elements (arrows 1 → A) are "not essential", because category-theoretic objects need not be structured sets. His examples are sheaves of Einstein algebras for GR with asymptotic boundary conditions, which may lack global sections (§3), and nCob and Hilb (§4). He concludes that ROSR "avoids the charge that it rests on an incoherent claim" (p. 1634). The paper never mentions the Yoneda lemma, representable functors or universal properties by name. | Read |
| [NOTE-194](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-194.md) | No categorial support for radical ontic structural realism | Lam and Wüthrich argue that category theory gives radical OSR no support. Identifying objects with identity arrows is relabelling (§3). Generalized elements X → A exist in every category, so elements are not eliminated (§4). Categories without products also lose set-style relations, "throwing out the relations with the relata" (§4). Morphisms relate C-objects, not the elements that stand for physical relata, and they "only distinguish isomorphism classes of structures" (§5). Bain's GR and TQFT cases eliminate at most spacetime points, not relata tout court (§§6–7). They conclude that category theory "offers little if any comfort to ROSR" (abstract) and favour "balanced" OSR. The Yoneda lemma is not named, although §§4–5 state two of its consequences. | Read |
| [NOTE-217](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-217.md) | Natural Kinds (SEP) | Whether scientific kinds are natural breaks into four questions (are the classifications natural, are they into kinds, what the kinds are, and do they have essences). The entry maps the positions from conventionalism to essentialist strong realism, notes a recent turn toward pluralist and epistemology-first views and even eliminativism, and questions whether Kripke–Putnam semantics can deliver essences. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-264](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-264.md) | I. Taking Ourselves Seriously; II. Getting It Right | Frankfurt grounds practical reason and normativity in the will rather than in reason. Reflexive self-division makes higher-order attitudes possible (pp. 170–171). Identification, a largely default "willing acceptance" (p. 173), turns a desire from "a problem" into a reason (p. 175). Free will is "volitional unanimity" between the governing desire and higher-order volitions (p. 177), and caring is wanting to go on wanting (p. 180). Final ends and their normative authority come from love, "strictly volitional" (p. 196): its involuntary, wholehearted "volitional necessities" are "irresistible, but … not coercive" (p. 197) and are "the only legitimate authority" for our normative convictions (p. 201). The 1971 wanton/person taxonomy is gestured at in a single phrase and its apparatus is not restated. | Read |
| [NOTE-265](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-265.md) | What Happens When Someone Acts? | Velleman argues that the "standard story" of action (desire + belief cause an intention, which causes movement) leaves the agent out. It fails even when every causal link is normal: his example is an intention to end a friendship, formed and executed without him (p. 104). Frankfurt's hierarchical remedy cannot fix it either. Any mental item picked out without presupposing the agent's participation (a second-order desire, a Watsonian value, a "decisive commitment") is one the agent can be alienated from. Any item defined so as to guarantee participation begs the question of agent-causation (pp. 112–116). His alternative is to look for what is *functionally identical* to the agent, not what the agent identifies with. That can only be a motive always behind and never merely in front of critical reflection: the desire to act in accordance with reasons. Its reinforcing force is the agent's contribution (pp. 117–122). | Read |
| [NOTE-267](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-267.md) | Personal Autonomy | The entry sorts accounts of self-government into four families: "coherentist" (hierarchical desires, Frankfurt; evaluative judgments, Watson; plans, Bratman; caring; character), reasons-responsive, responsiveness-to-reasoning (Christman, Mele) and incompatibilist, with relational conditions as a compatible add-on. It then argues (§3) that none of them, alone or combined, gives the *minimal* conditions of autonomy. Coherence is not sufficient, because the endorsement itself can be manipulated. It is not necessary either: a weak-willed agent, or someone acting against her plans, still governs herself. And any attempt to ground identification in some attitude restarts the regress. The only attitude no agent can be alienated from, the desire to be self-governing, cannot be the criterion, because it is present even in failures. The 1971 hierarchy gets one sentence, and Frankfurt's later replies (decisive commitment, then "satisfaction") get one footnote. | Read |
| [NOTE-269](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-269.md) | Moral Responsibility and the Principle of Alternative Possibilities | PAP ("a person is morally responsible for what she has done only if she could have done otherwise") has no decisive positive argument: it is not self-evident, and the moral arguments from fairness, OIC and the W-defense cover blame at most. Frankfurt-style cases (FSCs) are the strongest attack, because the factor that makes the act inevitable plays no role in producing it. The entry lays out three defences of PAP: - general-ability readings (PAP-general); - "flickers of freedom", which Fischer answers with the robustness requirement; - the Kane/Widerker/Ginet dilemma, answered by Fischer's causal-irrelevance reply on the first horn and by Pereboom's buffer case, Hunt's blockage and Mele & Robb 1998 on the second. Robb reports "not much consensus" (§5). He treats the fall of PAP as re-energising compatibilism, with Frankfurt's 1971 identification view and Fischer & Ravizza's guidance control as the two replacement accounts. | Read |
| [NOTE-270](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-270.md) | Compatibilism | The entry sorts compatibilism by which incompatibilist premise it denies: that free will requires the ability to do otherwise, that determinism precludes it, or that free will requires ultimate sourcehood. It argues that every "mesh" compatibilism has the same weak point: its sufficient conditions (hierarchies, reasons-responsive mechanisms, values) can be installed by manipulation, so each must either show what is wrong with manipulation cases or accept them. Its §4.2.1 is the fullest statement of Frankfurt 1971 in this batch. It covers first- and second-order desires, the will as the "effective first-order desire" that moves one "all the way to action" (1971, p. 84, Watson-1982 reprint pagination), the therapist's mere second-order desire versus a second-order volition (pp. 84–5), the unwilling and willing addicts, and "One acts of her own free will if and only if her action issues from the will she wants." The current revision has **dropped the wanton/person distinction**. The 2004–2015 revisions had it ("passive bystanders to their wills", 1971, p. 89) and have to be read for it. | Read |
| [NOTE-297](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-297.md) | Structural Realism: The Best of Both Worlds? | Worrall argues that the only position that honours both the no-miracles argument and the historical fact of radical theoretical change is Poincaré's "structural or syntactic realism". What survives theory change and explains predictive success is mathematical structure: equations carried over unchanged (Fresnel's reflection/refraction amplitude ratios, reinterpreted as electric-vector amplitudes in Maxwell's theory) or recovered as limiting cases under the correspondence principle (Newton from Einstein). The underlying ontology (elastic ether versus electromagnetic field) is not what survives. The support is one worked case and a general appeal to the correspondence principle. There are no formal definitions, and the paper says itself that "much clarificatory work needs to be done", above all on what it is for one theory's structure to approximate another's (p. 121). | Read |
| [NOTE-335](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-335.md) | Putnam — Psychological Predicates | Pain is hypothesised to be a functional state of a whole organism, a probabilistic automaton's state fixed by its machine table, rather than a physical-chemical brain state, because a functional organisation common to all pain-feelers is a likelier invariant than a physical one. The hypothesis carries the anti-nesting condition (3): no pain-feeler has a decomposition into parts that separately possess the pain-capable kind of Description. Its only stated motive is to exclude swarms of bees. Its clause (1) is empty, since everything is a probabilistic automaton under some Description. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-336](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-336.md) | Chalmers — Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness | The easy problems of consciousness are problems of explaining functions, which a mechanism explains; the hard problem is that "why is the performance of these functions accompanied by experience?" survives the explanation of every function. The argument is conceptual: the easy phenomena are functionally definable and experience is not. The positive part takes experience as fundamental and proposes structural coherence and organizational invariance as nonbasic psychophysical principles, with a double-aspect theory of information as a speculative basic one. Nothing is measured; the invariance argument is a one-page sketch. | Read |
| [NOTE-338](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-338.md) | Where Am I? | A first-person story with an argument inside. With his brain in a vat in Houston radio-linked to his body under Tulsa, the narrator tests three answers to "where am I?": where the body is, where the brain is, where the point of view is. He favours the third and finds it unclear. A computer duplicate of his brain can take over his body with no detectable difference, and when duplicate and brain drift out of step there are two persons in one body. Intuition pumps, no thesis defended to the end. | Read |
| [NOTE-340](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-340.md) | List — What is it like to be a group agent? | A short, conditional argument. Group agents are real by a thin functionalist definition and a naturalistic indispensability argument, and they have consciousness as awareness. Phenomenal consciousness turns on a bridge principle. Agency-, biology- and information-based principles are surveyed, and IIT is adopted. Three structural reasons (functional decomposability, robustness of steering bodies to partial randomisation, processing done mainly inside members) are said to make a group's Φ low. The exclusion postulate is a second route. Nothing is computed. The result is used to ground a normative asymmetry: group agents have only derivative rights. | Read |
| [NOTE-342](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-342.md) | Chalmers — Does a rock implement every finite-state automaton? | Implementation needs strong, counterfactual-supporting conditionals for every transition in the table, not one run, so Putnam's rock does not implement every FSA. Repaired, the triviality result survives for weak formalisms. A clock plus a dial implements every inputless FSA. The right input–output dependencies plus an input memory and a dial implement every FSA with those dependencies. Combinatorial-state automata, with independently varying components in distinct physical regions, demand fine-grained causal structure, and a blind implementation must grow exponentially. Logically possible false implementations and an overstrict independence condition are left open. Minds attach to (system, CSA) pairs, so the Chinese room holds two. | Read |
| [NOTE-346](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-346.md) | Dennett — Facing Backwards on the Problem of Consciousness | A three-page reply to Chalmers's "Facing Up". The easy/hard split misdirects research: a vitalist could pose the same hard problem of life, and a hard problem of perception set aside from its "easy" parts would be an artifact. Chalmers's reason why experience differs restates the claim. Subtracting every function from one's own consciousness leaves nothing but a conviction. Adding experience to physics' fundamentals would need independent evidence, which is absent. Argument by analogy, with one introspective premise. | Read |
| [NOTE-347](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-347.md) | Chalmers — Absent Qualia, Fading Qualia, Dancing Qualia | Organizational invariance, that fine-grained functional isomorphs of a conscious system have the same experiences, is defended by reductio over gradual neuron replacement. Absent qualia would imply a rational being systematically wrong about its own fading experience. Inverted or absent qualia would imply experience that flips with a switch and cannot be noticed. Both are judged implausible, not impossible. The paper extends the argument to a population of homunculi and to a single record-keeping homunculus. The conclusion is natural, not metaphysical, supervenience of experience on organisation, and it says nothing about systems that are not isomorphs. | Read |
| [NOTE-353](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-353.md) | True Believers: The Intentional Strategy and Why It Works | Belief is objective but visible only through a strategy: a true believer is any system "reliably and voluminously predictable" by treating it as a rational agent with the beliefs and desires it ought to have. Adopting the stance is free; its success is a fact, and Laplacean Martians who skipped it would miss real patterns. Thermostats and people differ in degree, by how tightly their states are tied to one interpretation. Evolution explains easily why the strategy works; how the machinery does it is open, and the language of thought is a bet, not a necessity. | Read |
| [NOTE-354](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-354.md) | Chalmers — The Meta-Problem of Consciousness | The meta-problem, why we judge that consciousness poses a hard problem, is an easy problem to be solved in topic-neutral terms. The paper surveys thirteen mechanisms and favours introspective models that attribute primitive relations of acquaintance to primitive qualities. It then poses a meta-problem challenge: a theory's basis of consciousness should explain our judgments about consciousness, which IIT and biological theories struggle to meet. It blocks debunking arguments for illusionism, but concedes a residual coincidence. It argues that only strong illusionism dissolves the hard problem, and rejects it by a Moorean argument. Nothing is measured; the solution offered is an explanandum sketch. | Read |
| [NOTE-356](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-356.md) | Chalmers — Extended Cognition and Extended Consciousness | Chalmers restates the 1998 extended-mind thesis as a claim about constitution through sensorimotor interaction, because the original statement is satisfied by wired-in "extended circuits" that the critics accept. He keeps the perception-action boundary as the strongest objection, and argues that consciousness does not extend because it needs information directly available for global control, and perception makes availability indirect. Both moves are proposed and defended against a few cases, not demonstrated. | Read |
| [NOTE-357](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-357.md) | Dennett — Quining Qualia | Qualia are supposed to be ineffable, intrinsic, private and directly apprehensible properties of experience. Fifteen intuition pumps argue that the pretheoretical concept is confused and that nothing has all four marks. The core move: an inversion in early processing and an inversion in memory-linked reactions are introspectively indistinguishable, so a subject has no privileged access to which happened. In place of qualia the paper offers practically ineffable, idiosyncratically detected public properties. It is argument by example throughout, and the author says so. | Read |
| [NOTE-358](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-358.md) | Chalmers — The combination problem for panpsychism | A taxonomy, not a solution. The combination problem is three problems (subject, quality, structure) plus four smaller ones (unity, boundary, awareness, grain). Each yields an argument against constitutive panpsychism, and subject-summing and structural mismatch are the strongest. Responses fall into emergent, autonomous, identity and combinatorial panpsychism. The non-combinatorial ones pay in mental causation or revised physics. Phenomenal bonding, quantum holism, small palettes and informational composition are judged most promising, but none is shown to work. James's argument at its origin is an argument against group minds, and a footnote objects to IIT's exclusion postulate that it makes consciousness extrinsic. | Read |
| [NOTE-362](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-362.md) v2 | Kammerer — How a materialist can deny that the US is probably conscious | The Sophisticated Anti-Nesting Principle. A whole W with a functional property P that would normally suffice for conscious state S lacks S if some part of W plays a role that (A) requires the part to have conscious states representing W and (B) is needed for W to have P (or any other property sufficient for S). The SAP leaves the antheads and Block's tiny-people brain conscious, permits some group consciousness, and denies the US conscious states because its citizens represent it and could not be replaced by parts that do not. Its defence is an Occam-style rule against ascribing consciousness where other subjects' states explain the behaviour, plus a tu quoque on residual arbitrariness. | Read |
| [NOTE-364](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-364.md) | The Self as a Center of Narrative Gravity | A self is an abstractum like a centre of gravity, posited by interpretation, and like a fictional character it is indeterminate beyond what its story fixes. A mindless novel-writing robot can author a self whose story is true of the robot. Brains are bundles of partly autonomous systems that make themselves cohere into one autobiography, and when the story coheres around two points there are two selves. The essay argues by analogy and thought experiment. Its evolutionary account of self-talk is speculation, and its evidence is cited. | Read |
| [NOTE-365](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-365.md) | Integrated Information Theory 3.0 | The 2014 restatement of IIT. Five axioms of experience become five postulates about mechanisms in a state, and an experience is identified with the maximally irreducible conceptual structure of a complex. Exclusion is the anti-nesting rule: of all overlapping sets of elements, only the one with locally maximal Φ is conscious, so no subset or superset of a complex is. It is postulated from the axiom that experience has definite borders; Occam's razor is invoked only for exclusion within a mechanism. Logic-gate examples give minor complexes, a conscious inactive network, a minimally conscious photodiode and a feed-forward zombie. Nothing larger than about a dozen elements is computable. | Read |
| [NOTE-366](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-366.md) | Block — Troubles with Functionalism | Functionalism fixes mental states only by their relations to inputs and outputs, so a body run by a billion radio-linked people, each executing one line of your machine table, is functionally equivalent to you. There is prima facie doubt that it has qualia, and Block argues the doubt has a rational basis: it is unlike us in psychology and neurophysiology, and it was built to mimic us. The doubt does not depend on the parts having minds. Putnam's anti-nesting stipulation is an ad hoc patch that fails in every version Block tries. Psychofunctionalism secures beliefs but perhaps not qualia, and no account of inputs and outputs avoids both liberalism and chauvinism. | Read |
| [NOTE-367](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-367.md) | Dennett & Kinsbourne — Time and the Observer | The Cartesian Theater is the tacit assumption that some place or moment in the brain makes contents conscious, so that arrival order there fixes experienced order. The Multiple Drafts model replaces it: discriminations are made once, locally, and revised in parallel; temporal order is represented by content, not by the timing of vehicles. Four timing "anomalies" then need no backward projection. At sub-second scales the difference between pre- and post-experiential revision is said to be only verbal. It is a conceptual argument over published data; no experiment is run. | Read |
| [NOTE-371](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-371.md) | Dennett — Reply to Professor Stich | Dennett accepts Stich's summary of Brainstorms and answers his three charges. The evolutionary grounding of rationality is deliberately minimal. Full rationality is an idealisation, irrationality has no stable description, and so personhood rests on a concept "we only imperfectly achieve". On pain, eliminativism and the reality of suffering are reconciled by policy: biting the bullet, reform and common sense each have uses, and Dennett stays with "there are no such things as pains, although of course people do feel pain". | Read |
| [NOTE-373](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-373.md) | Survival and Identity | What matters in survival is the R-relation (mental continuity and connectedness among person-stages), and it is also identity, because persons are maximal R-interrelated aggregates of stages and so the relation of being stages of one person is the R-relation. Fission and fusion become persons sharing stages, counted by tensed identity; the long-lived Methuselah is a continuum of overlapping persons; degrees come from supervaluation over cut-offs. Against Perry's lifetimes, two persons, not three, take part in a fission. | Read |
| [NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md) | Personal Identity | A survey of the persistence debate with an animalist's emphasis. It separates seven questions, argues that the persistence question concerns numerical identity and must not presuppose person essentialism, and sets out psychological-continuity, brute-physical and anticriterialist answers. Fission and the too-many-thinkers objection are the two arguments that do the work. It avoids the word "self". One in-text citation (Olson and Witt 2020) has no matching bibliography entry. | Read |
| [NOTE-376](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-376.md) | Shanahan — Palatable Conceptions of Disembodied Being | An avowedly "poetic" attempt to fit consciousness and selfhood to a disembodied 2024 chat agent. Its time would be discrete and discontinuous. Its "I" can be the model or a conversation-bound self that flickers into being each turn; we may slip between them. Such selves can be copied, edited and merged, and spread over branching simulacra. No candidate site survives scrutiny, which is read as Buddhist emptiness and applied back to human selves. Examples are invented usages, not data. | Read |
| [NOTE-378](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-378.md) | Personal Identity | Wiggins's division case shows that what matters in survival need not be one-one, so it is not identity; fusion and imagined beings that divide show it comes in degrees. Q-memory and q-intention describe the relations without presupposing identity. Continuity (transitive) is distinguished from connectedness (degree), and successive selves are proposed in place of one underlying person. The principle of self-interest then has no independent force. §I is argued; the priority of connectedness is asserted; §VI is a sketch. | Read |
| [NOTE-379](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-379.md) | Taylor — Consciousness interpreted | A charitable reconstruction, not a defence. Consciousness is a real pattern (Dennett 1991b) in the brain's content-bearing states, and a user-illusion, a pattern so coarse that describing the brain through it is unwitting metaphor. This makes six claims consistent: multiple drafts, global workspace, qualia eliminativism, user-illusion, fallibility and dictatorial authority. The Orwell/Stalin indeterminacy is rebuilt without verificationism: the two readings compress and predict equally, so neither better describes the pattern. | Read |
| [NOTE-381](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-381.md) | Schwitzgebel — Is the United States Phenomenally Conscious? Reply to Kammerer | Three concerns about Kammerer's Sophisticated Anti-Nesting Principle. It may not exclude actual groups, even the US, because citizens may not consciously represent the concrete entity at issue. Condition A's "required" makes group consciousness depend on members' motives: read loosely it gives flickering consciousness with no group-level change, read strictly it can never be met. The Occam-style justification either generalises into causal exclusion or is ad hoc, and group-level explanation is often simpler. Kammerer's is still the best anti-nesting principle the author has met. | Read |
| [NOTE-384](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-384.md) | Frankish — Illusionism as a Theory of Consciousness | Illusionism named and defended as a research programme. Phenomenal properties are not instantiated; the task is the illusion problem, to explain why experiences seem to have them. "Quasi-phenomenal" properties, the physical properties introspection misrepresents as phenomenal, separate strong illusionism from a weak illusionism that is argued to be unstable. The case is conservatism, the threat of epiphenomenalism, covert illusionism in reductive theories, a debunking argument and an abductive one from anomalousness. Objections are answered by agreeing to weakened versions of their intuitions. | Read |
| [NOTE-385](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-385.md) | Of Identity and Diversity | Identity is relative to the idea the name stands for: same mass, same life (oak, horse, man), same consciousness (person). A person is a thinking being that "can consider itself as itself", and personal identity reaches as far back as consciousness can be extended, independent of substance. Man and person come apart (prince and cobbler; day-man and night-man), and "person" is "a forensic term" grounding reward and punishment. Argued from cases and intuitions; "the same consciousness" is never defined. | Read |
| [NOTE-386](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-386.md) | Of Personal Identity | No impression of a self is constant, so there is no idea of one; introspection finds only perceptions, and the mind is "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". Its ascribed identity is a fiction of the imagination, like that of ships, churches and plants, produced by resemblance and causation, with memory discovering rather than producing it; hard cases are "grammatical". The Appendix confesses that two principles, the distinctness of perceptions and the imperceptibility of real connexions, leave the unity of the mind unexplained. | Read |
| [NOTE-387](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-387.md) | The Self and the Future | A body-exchange experiment told twice. Third-personally, with selfish choices before and reactions after, it supports "changing bodies". First-personally, as torture preceded by amnesia, character change and implanted memories, fear remains rational at every step, and the step that completes the exchange alters only what happens to someone else. Conceptual undecidability and conventional decision leave the subject unable to expect anything. A "rather shaky" lean toward the bodily answer, as a risk. | Read |
| [NOTE-388](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-388.md) | Social ontology: Some basic principles | Searle restates the 1995 theory in twenty pages. Social facts are facts involving collective intentionality. Institutional facts are the subclass in which collective acceptance imposes a status function, "X counts as Y in C", carrying deontic powers that give desire-independent reasons for action. Language is constitutive, since such facts exist only as represented. He revises the book in two places: status indicators matter in their own right, and some Y terms are free-standing, with no X, as with corporations and money without currency. "We accept (S has power (S does A))", a formula from later in the book, is now ranked as the more general form. Collective intentionality is assumed, not argued for. | Read |
| [NOTE-389](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-389.md) | Ritchie — Social Structures and the Ontology of Social Groups | A structuralist framework for social groups. A social structure is a network of relations constitutively dependent on social factors; it can be overt or covert, intentionally or unintentionally created and instantiated, internal or external to what realizes it. Organized social groups are structured wholes whose internal social structures people occupy; feature social groups are social kinds, nodes in external social structures, which can be intersectional. A restriction to structures that intuitively exist or figure in explanations keeps arbitrary collections out. Motivated, not proved; nothing on agency or minds. | Read |
| [NOTE-390](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-390.md) | Ritchie — What are groups? | Six criteria for any theory of groups (members vary across times and worlds; groups are temporary, contingent and located; coincident groups of one kind can be distinct) rule out groups as non-singular pluralities, fusions, Burge aggregates and Effingham's sets. Proposed: a group is a realization of a structure whose nodes are defined by functional relations; it exists while every node is occupied, members are the occupiers, and two groups are identical at a time only with the same members in the same relations. A sketch of a view, silent on agency. | Read |
| [NOTE-391](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-391.md) | Durkheim — Qu'est-ce qu'un fait social ? | Defines the social fact by exteriority to individual consciousness and external constraint, shown by sanction or by resistance, with diffusion plus independent existence as an equivalent test. Social facts are neither organic nor individual-psychic, so their substrate is society; they are general because collective, and "in each part because in the whole". Statistics isolates collective currents from individual cases. Ways of being are consolidated ways of doing. All of it is definition and illustration; the elimination that yields "a new species" is assumed exhaustive. | Read |
| [NOTE-393](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-393.md) | Epstein — Social Ontology (SEP) | A survey organised by its author's own distinction: what grounds a social fact versus what anchors the category it falls under. It reports that ontological individualism is widely assumed and now contested; that grounding has displaced supervenience; that convention, collective acceptance, patterns, practices and language are rival theories of anchoring; and that whether anchoring is a distinct relation is disputed. It covers groups, group agency, institutions, race and gender, artifacts, money, law and language. Survey claims are reported, not argued; one citation (Epstein 2016) is missing from the bibliography, and Schwitzgebel 2015 is listed with critics of group phenomenal states. | Read |
| [NOTE-394](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-394.md) | Haslanger — Gender and Race: (What) Are They? | An explicitly ameliorative ("analytical") account. Gender and race are defined as hierarchical social positions: a woman is someone regularly observed or imagined to have bodily features presumed to indicate a female's reproductive role, marked by that within the dominant ideology for subordinate positions, and subordinated in part because of it. Racialized groups are defined in parallel from features presumed to show ancestral links to a region. Gender in general and ethnicity are the non-hierarchical genus. The commonality and normativity objections are met by appeal to the project's values. Stipulative, with no evidence. | Read |
| [NOTE-424](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-424.md) v2 | Time, Structure and Fluctuations | Prigogine's Nobel statement. Near equilibrium δ²S < 0 with ½∂δ²S/∂t = P > 0 makes δ²S a Lyapounov function, and in the strictly linear regime (constant L_ρρ′) the steady state minimizes entropy production. Far from equilibrium ½∂δ²S/∂t = ΣδJ_ρδX_ρ has no fixed sign, and ΣδJδX ≥ 0 is offered only as a sufficient stability condition. The Brusselator goes unstable at B > 1 + A². Dissipative structures are instabilities of the thermodynamic branch, triggered by fluctuations and sustained by exchange with the outside. The microscopic §§6–7 is a programme, linked to macroscopic thermodynamics only "in the linear region". | Read |
| [NOTE-432](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-432.md) | Explanatory Models for Psychiatric Illness | Psychiatric etiology is multilevel, non-aggregative and full of causal loops, so law-based explanation fails and so do both hard reduction and hard emergence. Mechanistic explanation proceeds by local decomposition and difficult reassembly. Following Marr, biology implements the functions psychology describes and does not replace them. The argument is philosophical, illustrated by an alcohol-dependence sketch and cited findings; it reports no data of its own. | Read |
| [NOTE-441](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-441.md) | Self-Regulation and the Problem of Human Autonomy: Does Psychology Need Choice, Self-Determination, and Will? | SDT's autonomy is "regulation by the self": acting with reflective endorsement, graded along the internalization continuum, compatible with external influence, dependence and a single option. Ryan and Deci align it with phenomenological and hierarchical (Frankfurt, Dworkin) accounts and use that definition to answer behaviourist, social-cognitive, reductionist, nonconscious-priming, choice-overload and cultural critiques. Autonomy lies not in being an uncaused cause but in the capacity to "reflectively endorse or reject prompted actions" (p. 1573). | Read |
| [NOTE-447](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-447.md) | The Emperor's New Markov Blankets | Pearl blankets (conditional-independence shields in a Bayesian network) and Friston blankets (agent–environment boundaries in the world) are different constructs conflated in the free-energy literature. The four-way partition needs a chosen internal node, sensorimotor labels and steady state; in Friston's soup it also needs electrochemical-only coupling and a fixed cluster size. Realist use needs metaphysical premises; instrumental use is innocent but settles nothing about boundaries. | Read |
| [NOTE-455](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-455.md) | The Normative Constitution of Agency | Korsgaard asks whether agency is natural (a movement caused by the right mental state) or normatively constituted (a movement backed by an agent whose unity is achieved by following norms). Ordinary attribution of action implies activity and identity. Self-constitution explains both: the categorical and hypothetical imperatives give action the form of self-determined efficacy, and the maxims chosen under them constitute practical identity. Reflective self-consciousness breaks given unity and sets the task of rebuilding it, so unity of agency is "an achievement, not a given". | Read |
| [NOTE-460](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-460.md) | Précis: Being No One | Metzinger's own sketch of the self-model theory. Six constraints (globality, presentationality, transparency, convolved holism, dynamicity, perspectivalness) build up consciousness; a transparent self-model yields phenomenal selfhood, so "no such things as selves exist in the world"; transparency is graded, inversely proportional to the attentional availability of earlier processing stages. Phenomenal unity is one global functional cluster. The first-person perspective is a model of the intentionality relation, whose iteration gives introspective and social intelligence. A theory statement: no new evidence. | Read |
| [NOTE-468](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-468.md) | Biological organisation as closure of constraints | A constraint acts on a process while being conserved at that process's time scale; closure is a set of constraints, each directly dependent on and generative for another, that cannot be split. This separates closure from cycles of processes, grounds functions, and gives a boundary criterion, refined by a preliminary count-based tendency to closure for symbionts and by nested separated closures for levels. Applied only to schematic examples; closure is not claimed to define organisms. | Read |
| [NOTE-490](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-490.md) | Block — The Mind as the Software of the Brain | An introductory chapter that says what the computer model of the mind claims and defends it. Intelligence is explained by functional decomposition into primitive processors; meaning-respecting processing by an isomorphism between syntactic and semantic functions that must hold counterfactually; intentionality by a language of thought whose symbols get meaning from functional role. The Turing test, Stich's syntactic theory and Searle's Chinese room are criticised. Block grants the model for intelligence and intentionality and doubts it for phenomenal consciousness. | Read |
| [NOTE-491](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-491.md) | Block & Fodor — What Psychological States are Not | Block and Fodor argue that behaviourism and type physicalism fail on empirical grounds, and that machine-state functionalism (FSIT) fails because psychological states cannot be one-to-one with the machine-table states of a probabilistic automaton. Dispositions, simultaneity, productivity and structure all break the correspondence, and machine-table identity is too fine-grained. Inverted and absent qualia are a prima facie objection to any functional definition. What survives is that psychological states may be computational states of an automaton, typed by the laws they fall under. | Read |
| [NOTE-501](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-501.md) | The Harder Problem of Consciousness | An argument for a conditional. If naturalism (physicalism is the default), phenomenal realism and anti-scepticism hold, then whether a superficial functional isomorph with a different physical basis is conscious is meta-inaccessible. Physicalism is then the default yet inaccessible, and it is the subjective default that the isomorph is not conscious while the question stays open. Disjunctive and superficial-role identities are metaphysically possible but could never be accepted by inference to the best explanation. | Read |
| [NOTE-504](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-504.md) | Block — Inverted Earth | Block gives the converse of the inverted spectrum: on Inverted Earth a subject or twin with identical brain, identical qualitative content and no internal disturbance comes, through his embedding in the environment and language, to have inverted intentional content and an inverted long-arm functional role. So qualitative content is not a functional state, and public colour talk expresses intentional content. The argument is stronger than the inverted spectrum on testimony and supervenience. A short-arm functional theory of qualia would escape it, and Block can only ask what that theory is. | Read |
| [NOTE-505](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-505.md) | Comparing the Major Theories of Consciousness | Compares higher-order thought, global workspace and biological theories by whether they can recognise the explanatory gap. HOT and the workspace replace it with puzzles of their own making; only the biological theory fully acknowledges it, and concept dualism (Nagel, Loar) keeps it from implying dualism. Ambitious HOT also suffers ad hoc stipulation, the mismatch problem and implausibility for infants. Goldberg et al.'s data suggest self-related activity is inhibited in intense perception. The biological theory is the least friendly to machine consciousness. | Read |
| [NOTE-506](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-506.md) | Block — Psychologism and Behaviorism | A machine that stores every sensible conversation of a given length and looks up its next reply has the capacity to respond sensibly to anything said to it, so it meets the strongest behaviourist conception of intelligence, but its intelligence is its programmers'. So psychologism is true: whether behaviour is intelligent depends partly on how it is produced. The standard objections to behaviourism only ever refuted necessary conditions; this refutes the sufficient one. Psychologism does not require our kind of processing, only processing that is not of the most elementary sort. | Read |
| [NOTE-511](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-511.md) | Block — Mental Paint | Block defends phenomenism, the view that phenomenal character outruns representational content, against both forms of representationism. Internalist representationism has only functional resources, and a child raised among ever-changing colours has colour experiences without abiding functional differences. Externalist representationism fails on swampman, on the difference between attention and awareness, on bodily sensations, on Inverted Earth with intact long-term memory, and on an empirical shifted-spectrum argument from normal variation in colour vision. What stays the same across representational change is mental paint. | Read |
| [NOTE-545](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-545.md) | Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person | Persons differ from other creatures in the structure of the will: they have second-order volitions, desires that a given desire be the one that moves them to act, and wantons do not. Forming one is identifying with a desire. Freedom of the will is having the will one wants, and a decisive identification ends the series of higher orders "without cutting it off arbitrarily" (p. 16). Responsibility needs neither a free will nor alternatives: the willing addict acts of his own free will. The view is neutral on determinism, and on how the will came to be (n. 10). | Read |
| [NOTE-546](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-546.md) | Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility | Frankfurt argues that PAP is false because circumstances can make an action unavoidable without bringing it about: Black stands ready to make Jones4 act and never needs to, so Jones4 is as responsible, for blame or praise, as he would be without Black (§IV). A fact that explains nothing about the action cannot excuse it (§V). The replacement principle excuses only an agent who acted "only because he could not have done otherwise", and Frankfurt says it is compatible with determinism. | Read |
| [NOTE-550](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-550.md) | List & Pettit — Group Agency and Supervenience | Four conditions of agency (§2). A group's judgments supervene on members' contributions under a constitution (§3). With a universal domain, robust group rationality is inconsistent with majoritarian, uniform proposition-wise and proposition-wise supervenience (Propositions 1–3), and consistent with set-wise supervenience, as the premise-based and distributed premise-based procedures show (Propositions 4–5; Table 4). The group's judgment on a conclusion can be fixed by members' judgments on premises alone. Emergent agency without members' conception of the group is judged unintelligible (§6). | Read |
| [NOTE-554](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-554.md) | List — Three kinds of collective attitudes | Aggregate attitudes: a rule or market summarises members' attitudes; proposition-wise supervenience; no direct role; rationality contingent (majority beliefs on p, q, p∧q can be inconsistent, Table 1). Common attitudes: all hold, with common awareness; enriched proposition-wise supervenience; coordination; consistent by unanimity. Corporate attitudes: a group agent's; holistic supervenience, like non-reductive physicalism; action-guiding; rationality presupposed. Three lessons of near-independence; Table 2 summarises. | Read |
| [NOTE-560](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-560.md) | Nonreductive Physicalism and the Limits of the Exclusion Principle | With causes as proportional difference-makers, Kim's exclusion principle fails. A revised principle (a property and its realizer never both cause an effect) is true of some systems and false of others. A higher-level property excludes its realizer as cause exactly when the effect is realization-insensitive, surviving nearby changes of realizer. That is plausibly the norm in the special sciences, which makes higher-level causes autonomous. | Read |
| [NOTE-585](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-585.md) | Causation and Manipulability | A survey of manipulability theories that states Woodward's own. X causes Y iff some intervention on X with respect to Y would change Y, where an intervention is a surgical, exogenous cause of X meeting conditions M1–M4. The account is non-reductive but not viciously circular, needs no human agent, and defines total, direct and contributing causes by combinations of interventions. Invariance and higher-level causation are not discussed. | Read |
